#1026. What Germany thinks of carmaker Audi's $4 billion deal with Trump

The luxury carmaker is set to open its first factory in the United States — a move Trump credits to his tariffs. DW examines the German reaction amid a massive auto industry cull at home.

US President Donald Trump announced the investment on Saturday, during a campaign rally in Georgia, a key battleground state for his Republican Party in the midterm elections next week.

Audi quickly confirmed the plan, saying it would build its first US factory near Macon, Georgia, costing around $4 billion (€3.6 billion) and creating some 4,500 jobs.

The German automaker said construction would begin next year, with a planned annual production of up to 200,000 vehicles due to start in the early 2030s.

The firm plans to build premium SUVs for the US market at the plant, marking a "long-term commitment" to what it said was "one of the world's most important premium markets."

The US investment comes as German automakers face unprecedented pressure from China, rising costs and two conflicts.

Backed by huge government subsidies, Chinese rivals have stolen a march in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), scaling up production of new models that are fast gaining market share in a crowded global auto market.

BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Audi's parent company, Volkswagen— the world's second-largest automaker — have all issued profit warnings in recent months as margins come under pressure.

They've also announced major cost-cutting. VW is preparing to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, while Audi's factory in Neckarsulm, which has around 15,000 staff, is one of four plants at risk of closure.

Trump credited his 15% tariffs on European-made vehicles for Audi's investment, saying it "would not have happened without tariffs."

While the commitment does feed into Trump's plan to bring manufacturing back to the United States from abroad, Audi said it was making the huge outlay for growth and resilience.

“We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," said the carmaker's CEO Gernot Döllner, who appeared alongside Trump at the Republican's campaign rally.

"The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that ... This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory," he said.

However, Trump's tariffs have undoubtedly added to the automaker's woes.

Audi, which currently exports to the US market from Europe and Mexico, said the additional costs amounted to about €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) last year.

With more than 160,000 vehicles sold, Audi's US sales last year fell 16%, amid intense competition and after Trump scrapped subsidies on electric vehicles in its second-biggest market.

By building a US factory, Audi should be able to avoid or reduce Trump's tariffs, industry analysts say.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There's been fierce criticism of the deal due to the severe pressure facing German automakers and because the new US investment could mean further job losses at home.

Much of the criticism focused on Döllner's rally appearance alongside Trump.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)'s transport policy spokesperson Isabel Cademartori described it as campaign assistance for an autocrat who is waging a trade war against Germany.

"This is a disgrace, especially considering the history of the Volkswagen Group," she stated, referring to the company's links with Adolf Hitler's Nazi party during World War II.

Christiane Benner, president of the powerful IG Metall union, labeled the rally appearance as "extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and not worthy of the company."

VW works council chief Daniela Cavallo went further, saying Döllner had let himself be turned "into a puppet in [Trump's] propaganda show."

Cavallo, however, noted that the US plant could make sense from a business perspective, as VW needs to grow its market share there.

An Audi spokesperson defended the US investment, saying it was "not a decision against Germany, but rather a step toward strengthening our global competitiveness."

Manfred Döss, chairman of Audi's supervisory board, insisted the automaker's future cannot be secured by cost-cutting and efficiency alone.

"We need the courage to invest, to seize new opportunities and to make decisions that will shape our company for decades to come," he added.

The announcement certainly appears timed to coincide with the US midterm elections on November 3.

Voters will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats hold the balance of power in Congress during Trump's last two years in office.

Holding the announcement in the key battleground state of Georgia is seen as a strategic move to boost the fortunes of local Republican candidates.

Since he returned to the White House last year, Trump has used tariffs and political pressure to force global automakers to relocate their factories to American soil.

Audi's investment follows moves by Stellantis and Japan's Toyota to expand US production, while Honda is in talks to build a new US plant.

US auto giants General Motors and Ford have also promised to increase domestic production.

While one investment announcement may not be enough to sway many voters, it serves one of Trump's main election promises — to revive industrial production in the US.

#1025. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

NO MISTAKE THIS TIME 💪 Bruno Fernandes gets United back in it after a penalty retake 😤 https://t.co/uQdkNs0lXo

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

From being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

At that point, the momentum was firmly in United’s favour and three minutes later they were in front. It is a source of bemusement among fans that Shea Lacey has not had more game-time considering how poor some senior players have been. And his arrival as a substitute made a big difference.

It was Lacey who speared an inch-perfect pass into Cunha, who turned sharply before drilling a stunning finish in off the near post. Cue bedlam.

The difference to those opening 45 minutes was as stark as it gets. Indeed, the first half felt like a continuation from the fans of their blood-letting against Bournemouth.

When the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

On the pitch, United were all over the place. Had he done, he would have seen Matías Soulé unmarked and in acres of space with Diogo Dalot, United’s left-back, caught high up the pitch. Soulé made no mistake with his finish.

At that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he said.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

“It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was important to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

“It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we showed what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”

“I said what can he do, I didn’t know where he would start, and he must have started in the dressing room, and pointing at a few people telling them to be brave and courageous and move the ball quicker, and run in behind and they did all those things in the second half and got their reward by getting their win.”

For the first time in months, United fans have witnessed a performance worth cheering (at least in the second half).

As Michael Carrick led his players around the pitch – with the occasional smile and fist pump – they were all greeted by cheers and applause in the stands. Some of them might have forgotten what that was like.

United fans are throwing tennis balls on the pitch and chanting “We want Glazers” out – the 20.05 minute protest in a nod to 2005, the year the Americans bought the club. “Sell United and f--- off home,” the Stretford End sings. Mayhem on and off the pitch.

Yellow cards for Bruno Fernandes and Matías Soulé as the two players exchange strong words and a shove.

Rensch went down and Roma players were screaming for the United players to put the ball out of play but they don’t.

Dalot caught in possession and the ball is picked off again. Roma make another run at goal and it’s blocked in the box but United are looking very shaky at the back.

He steps up to the spot and cool as you like send Lammens the wrong way to find the back of the net on the keeper’s right.

Malen makes it TWO-NIL ROMA from the spot, after a handball from Heaven in the box 😬 https://t.co/kUeOeQNRES

United are in real trouble when they lose the ball. Again they are carved open and Mora takes the ball down the left, sending another looping ball across the field. Soulé tries to find Malen making the run in the box but he can’t quite reach it.

It rebounds at the feet of Soulé and Heaven concedes a penalty for a handball

No shots or shots on target for United. One shot on target for Roma and one goal.

But Bruno Fernandes picks the ball up on the right wing from Diallo and fizzes a low ball across the face of goal. Mbeumo can’t quite connect and it is swept away from the feet of Cunha at the far post before he can tap it in.

This is obviously the last thing United would have wanted. The crowd – previously cheering every ball forward and every challenge – have gone quite quiet.

But just like that, Roma get the breakthrough.

United lose the ball and are carved open. Mora sends a long ball across the field and finds Soulé completely unmarked on the edge of the box. He brings it down, makes a short run and slots it past Lammens low at the near post.

THAT DIDN'T TAKE LONG 😬 United fall behind after just 11 minutes as Roma score through Matías Soulé 🇦🇷 https://t.co/DtIOFJYZ6D

Mainoo sends a nice pass out to Diallo on the right who sends a ball to Bruno Fernandes on the overlap. His ball into the box is quickly blocked but Mainoo has started very brightly and draws a foul in the next passage of play.

Bruno Fernandes sends a long ball downfield trying to set Mbeumo free but he can’t quite bring it down and control it, and Roma are back on the ball.

Cristante tries to slip a ball through to Malen in the centre of the box but it’s cleared away quickly.

The Netherlands international picks up the ball again and is quickly swarmed before he can turn in the box. United staying disciplined so far.

Yoro wins the ball in midfield and United get a bit of possession up the field but a sloppy pass from Dalot gifts it back to Roma and now the visitors are probing the United final third.

But in great news for United, they have reached four minutes without conceding, which is a feat they had not achieved in their last two European games.

Lammens is not taking any chances playing out from the back though, opting for the long ball out every time.

Mainoo tries to lift a ball over the top from midfield for Diallo on the right-hand side, but he doesn’t quite get it right.

An early goal would definitely boost spirits here. United are enjoying a spell on the ball and that will suffice for now.

United need to get off to a steady start here, conceding an early goal could be devastating.

There’s a minute of silence before play in memory of Jesus de ​Miguel who died on Tuesday morning.

As the Champions League anthems plays, fans have released their yellow and green balloons from the stands in protest against the club’s owners.

A mix of boos and cheers from around the ground.

We are five minutes out and both teams are lined up in the tunnel.

One banner in the stands reads “We’ll support you evermore”.

We’re about to see what the players can muster to earn that support.

With kick-off fast approaching, here’s a reminder of the teams taking to the field tonight:

Man Utd XI (4-2-3-1): Lammens; Dalot, Yoro, Maguire, Heaven; Baleba, Mainoo; Diallo, Cunha, Fernandes; Mbeumo

Subs: Darlow, Heaton, Amass, De Ligt, Martinez, Mazraoui, Santos, Mount, T Fletcher, Tielemans, Lacey, Zirkzee

AS Roma XI (3-4–2-1): Vazquez; Mancini, Balerdi, Hermoso; Rensch, Cristante, De Roon, Wesley; Soule, Rodrigo Mora; Malen

Subs: De Marzi, Koulierakis, N’Dicka, Castro, Molina, Pisilli, Di Nunzio, Lulli, Ghilardi

Bad timing with injuries means that tonight is the first time that Kobbie Mainoo and Carlos Baleba feature in midfield together.

Baleba was injured when he completed his £70m move from Brighton and Mainoo picked up his muscle injury as his team-mate returned to the substitutes bench.

It will be down to the two young players to stop Roma lacing balls through midfield to Malen and Carrick will need them to click on first time of trying.

Wayne Rooney has decided not to pull any punches tonight when it comes to his former club as he debates the possibility of a new manager arriving at Old Trafford.

“I’ll tell you Gabby with that group of players, none of the [possible replacement] managers are getting any more out of these players. The biggest job is getting them all out of the football club, that’s the biggest job,” he said to Gabby Logan.

The United manager has had his turn speaking to Amazon Prime with a very relaxed demeanour, despite the huge pressure sitting on his shoulders.

"It's a BIG night for us" 🗣️ Carrick gives his thoughts ahead of taking on Roma live on Prime 📺 https://t.co/BHFyKF4fXA

The former Aston Villa striker has hit the ground running in his first full season with Roma, and has already raced to eight goals and an assist in nine Serie A matches. He notched 14 goals in 18 league matches in the second half of last season while on loan, and has picked up where he left off.

He’s already scored three in the Champions League, and could be looking eagerly at United’s shaky mentality to add to those numbers. He is the top scorer in Europe’s top five leagues in this calendar year, beating the likes of Lamine Yamal and Harry Kane.

Gasperini’s man-to-man style emphasises his skill in one-on-one situations, where his pace and drive with the ball make him a handful for even the best defenders.

Here is the full list of tonight’s fixtures:

Matchday 4 is here ⚽️ #UCL https://t.co/tgJlzmaDAh

Galatasaray are already 2-0 up on Stuttgart, while Sporting have found the breakthrough against Shakhtar Donetsk in the early kick-offs.

Manchester United fans are planning a series of in-stadium demonstrations at Old Trafford tonight in protest at the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s ownership.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been plans to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No new stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

The Glazers and Ratcliffe have come under growing attack this season with the club’s regular match going supporters at war with the owners.

A separate fans’ group has also been encouraging fans to join in anti Glazers and Ratcliffe chants in the 21st minute or, more specifically, after 20 minutes and 5 seconds: 20.05 is a nod to 2005, the year the Glazers completed their hostile takeover at Old Trafford.

The main surprise for Roma is in goal, as with first-choice keeper Svilar out already, it has been confirmed that backup keeper Pierluigi Gollini has injured his back today. He has been replaced by Colombian Devis Vásquez in goal.

Roma: Vásquez; Balerdi, Mancini, Hermoso; Rensch, de Roon, Mora, Wesley; Soulé, Cristante; Malen

We have confirmation, Martínez is on the bench. He is replaced by Ayden Heaven while Bruno Fernandes is still with the captain’s armband in midfield. Kobbie Mainoo gets the nod as he returns from injury, along with Mateus Cunha and Mason Mount.

Your United team for tonight's #UCL clash 👊 https://t.co/TD9F6RjeAB

Lisandro Martínez has been dropped by Michael Carrick in the wake of his red card madness against Chelsea.

The United manager has opted to pair Ayden Heaven in central defence with Harry Maguire for the Roma game with Martinez dropping to the bench.

The Argentina defender received a second yellow card for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face in Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at Chelsea when he was also culpable for the first goal.

Martinez has been in dire form this season and was fined and publicly apologised after publicly criticising director of football Jason Wilcox and the Old Trafford board in the wake of the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid.

Kobbie Mainoo returns to midfield after missing the last four games through injury.

Ayden Heaven has just come out to speak with Prime Video, which has led Gabby Logan to assume that means that Lisandro Martínez will not start for Michael Carrick tonight.

Speaking with her, former United legend Wayne Rooney has said the Argentine has “simply not been good enough” and should not necessarily feature again under Carrick.

When Alan Shearer was asked if he would include Martínez on a team sheet tonight, he did not mince his words, calling him a “liability”.

Ahead of the confirmed line-ups coming out shortly, there are certain players we know we will not be seeing today.

Patrick Dorgu (hamstring), Luke Shaw (unspecified) and Benjamin Sesko (shin) remain sidelined for United, while Marcus Rashford and Amad Diallo will be assessed before the match.

There are no new concerns for Gasperini after his side’s latest match, the 5-2 win over Udinese, but he remains unable to select Muhammed Bah (ACL), Paulo Dybala, Manu Kone (thigh), Lorenzo Pellegrini (thigh) and first-choice keeper Mile Svilar (stress fracture, foot).

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ

All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

They bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

It has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Feel free to drop us your score predictions in the comments – bragging rights on the line for the winner.

We’ll be bringing you team news, previews from the managers and more ahead of kick-off at 8pm!

#1022. England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or

The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.

The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.

The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.

Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.

The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.

Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.

At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.

"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.

Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.

"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.

Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.

"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."

Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.

He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.

The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.

Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.

She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.

Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.

Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.

Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.

Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.

Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

Andres Iniesta rose from La Masia to win everything for club and country, and become one of the greatest midfielders of all time. In his own words, he tells FourFourTwo what it was like

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Leaving my family at 12 years old was one of the hardest things I’ve ever experienced. Above all, I felt fear. I was moving from my hometown, Fuentealbilla, not far from Valencia, and I was going to be alone in Barcelona. I was joining La Masia, but my first night there was tough for everyone, including my family. I couldn’t stop crying, and my father wanted to come and take me back home. Luckily, my mother changed his mind. We had to give it a try. I never thought about having to return to Fuentealbilla if I didn’t make it, nor did I obsess over how far I might go in football. What kept running through my mind was that I was at one of the best clubs in the world – I had to fulfil my dream of becoming a footballer.

I owe so much to my father – his advice, everything. He was my inspiration, and the one who pushed me to go to Barcelona in the first place. My essence as a footballer aligned with Barcelona’s style of play, so it was relatively easy to adapt when I started training at La Masia. I had to develop and perfect the concepts, but having the ball, positional play, working as a unit, that was the style I’d always had as a child in Albacete’s junior categories.

At Barcelona, I grew and gained experience – when I reached the youth team, that’s when I felt that the dream to become a footballer truly became mine. That’s when I thought, ‘This is serious now’. When I started playing for Barcelona B, I was one of those 17-year-old guys I used to look up to with excitement when I arrived at 12. That’s when I realised that it could be my time, but I always approached it with the intention of enjoying it – training with Rivaldo, Pep Guardiola, Phillip Cocu, Xavi and Carles Puyol, when I got the chance to join in with the first-team squad.

Michael Laudrup was my first big idol. I used to watch him closely and try to learn from his movements and elegance. I was also fascinated by Guardiola, not because he came from La Masia, but because of how he played. As a midfielder, I saw his vision of the game, how he positioned himself on the field, how he thought ahead of everyone else.

My connection with Xavi grew organically, without forcing anything. It grew over time, as we got more chances to play together. Maybe people forget now, but there was a time when it was said that we were incompatible. A lot was said, but we proved the opposite. We grew up with the same footballing philosophy and understood the game in the same way. When I was in the youth academy, Xavi had already heard about me, as he’s four years older than me. When I joined the first team, things gradually clicked until we eventually understood each other with just a glance.

The first time I joined up with the first team was special. I remember it with great emotion.

Carles Naval, Barça’s legendary team delegate, called La Masia to tell me that the manager Llorenc Serra Ferrer wanted me to start training with them. I didn’t know what to do at that moment. I was trembling all over. I went days without speaking. I’d spent years looking at Camp Nou from the window of La Masia. Now I was close to making my debut.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

After that, Louis van Gaal returned for a second spell as Barça’s coach. He was brave during a delicate time in Barça’s history. I remember we had a Under 19 European Championship with Spain, and he told me that he wanted me to start training permanently with the team during pre-season.

A year later, Ronaldinho arrived. He was different, groundbreaking – it was magical to watch him play, not just in matches, but also in training. He had spectacular physical power and technical quality far beyond any other player. He arrived at a challenging time for the club and brought back the fans’ hope and smiles. There’s a clear before and after in Barça’s modern history thanks to Ronaldinho.

We won La Liga after six years, then the Champions League in 2006, although I have bittersweet memories of that final against Arsenal in Paris. The priority was to win the Champions League, but being on the bench hurt that night because, in my view, it wasn’t fair – even if in football, the sense of fairness is very subjective.

When I found out that I wouldn’t be starting though, I didn’t let it bring me down. That’s never been my mentality. At that moment, all I thought about was being ready when Frank Rijkaard decided to bring me on, and to help win the trophy, which I did, when we came from a goal down to win.

We laid the foundations for a successful Barça. Ronaldinho paved the way for another genius: Messi. I cherish the small details of playing with him, the routine that never really felt like a routine, partly because of the way Leo surprised you every day. Training with him was incredible. We experienced amazing times on the pitch and many titles together, but I’ll always remember countless days at the training ground doing drills with incredible speed and precision. Tac, tac, tac. It was astonishing, and I feel privileged to have shared so many years with him.

In 2008, Guardiola became manager. From the very beginning, I had a feeling it was going to be a complete success. Personally, it was incredible to know that Guardiola was going to take charge of the team. Internally, I felt an immense sense of commitment and conviction, an indescribable motivation. Anyone who’s had the chance to work alongside one of their idols will understand me.

It was a great opportunity, and we realised it quickly. Pep was more than ready, and he conveyed that to the group during the first pre-season we had in Scotland. It was the conviction he had when explaining how he wanted us to play. He had everything planned out – from the defence, the positioning of the midfielders, to what the forwards had to do. You could see progress after just a few training sessions. The group executed Guardiola’s vision perfectly.

There was a lot of noise and doubt from the outside though, after we lost the first league game of the season to Numancia, then drew with Racing Santander at Camp Nou. One day, spontaneously, I decided to go to his office to reassure him. “Pep, don’t worry, everything will be fine,” I told him.

It wasn’t premeditated or discussed with the other captains. Maybe I decided to visit Guardiola because of the individual commitment I felt. I was convinced that great work was being done – we could sense it day by day and in the friendlies we played. We felt comfortable with that idea and were happy. What I conveyed to him was how the group felt. We were doing things right, and the momentum would change.

We won everything that season. But to win that Champions League final in Rome, we first had to get past Chelsea in the semi-finals. The second leg at Stamford Bridge will stay with me forever. Have I ever thought about what would have happened if I hadn’t scored in the 93rd minute? Never, just in case!

My shot was instinctive because I didn’t really have time to think about the execution. The ball came to me perfectly, and I knew roughly how I wanted to strike it. Luckily, it went to the one spot where Petr Cech couldn’t reach it, which was almost miraculous, considering he was as big as the goal itself. That ball was pushed in by all of us.

Winning that Champions League felt much better than three years earlier, even though I played injured in that final against Manchester United. I couldn’t shoot because of the risk of tearing a muscle, but internally I told myself: “I can’t miss this final after the one in Paris.” It turned out incredibly, although I paid the price afterwards with several muscle injuries.

A year before that, I’d also become a European champion with Spain. With the national team too, we had immense confidence in a specific playing style, and players who represented it perfectly. I credit the coach Luis Aragones for that. My best memory is when Iker Casillas lifted the European Championship trophy. So many generations had tried, and we managed to do it.

From the outside, a footballer’s life may seem perfect, particularly when you’re winning so many trophies. But we also have our worries. We’re human beings, too. I picked up several injuries after winning the Champions League final in Rome, and my great childhood friend Dani Jarque passed away. All of that made me hit rock bottom, but I tried not to give up, and I had the ability and humility to ask for professional help. I accepted that, at that moment, I was being consumed, that I needed other tools to get back on my feet. If I hadn’t done that, I imagine that my career would have been different. My family was also a great support.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, we lost our opening match. Afterwards, the message wasn’t exactly just ‘stay calm’, because when you lose your first game at a World Cup, the rest of the group stage is played under pressure. But we felt we’d played well against Switzerland. If we’d played that game 10 times, we would have won nine, so all we could do was keep trying, not doubt ourselves, and trust that we had the team to move forward. That’s what happened, and we progressed all the way to the final.

It was a tough and uncomfortable final. Rarely do those kinds of matches turn out to be open and entertaining. The Netherlands changed their style of play because of the opponent they were facing. They played aggressively, they showed us a lot of respect. The match was intense.

Then in extra time, I scored the winner. It’s hard to put that feeling into words. The ball came to me from Cesc Fabregas, I controlled it, and time stopped. It was like a slow-motion action. I heard silence. Why? I don’t know. I suppose the experience and responsibility from so many years at the elite level taught me to face high-pressure situations like that more calmly. Maybe someone else wouldn’t have even controlled the ball. That was the moment for Spain’s history to change with that World Cup.

During that era of Spanish football, maybe one of us could have won the Ballon d’Or, but it’s not something I dwell on. Whoever wins it deserves to, especially if it was Messi. I’ve had the chance to attend many of those ceremonies, and of course, anyone would love to win it, but it’s not something that bothers me at all. The image of Xavi, Messi and me – three guys from La Masia – on the podium in 2010 was bigger than winning it. That was the real prize.

In 2011, we won another Champions League together, this time at Wembley, against Manchester United again. Wembley is a sacred place for Barcelona fans – it was where the club became European champions for the first time, in 1992.

Facing Manchester United gave even more weight to that final. I remember preparing for it in great detail. We’d just won La Liga, and had two weeks to focus on that night. We travelled to England earlier than usual. We knew how Manchester United played, how to exploit their weaknesses and we had everything memorised. We went into half-time drawing 1-1, but we felt completely in control. We were dominating, and everything was unfolding as we wanted. It was perfect, and eventually we won 3-1.

We won a lot during that era under Guardiola, even though in life you lose more than you win. In fact, I don’t even remember exactly how many titles we lifted. Looking back now, I realise how much effort it all took. Behind it all was a group of players with hunger and excitement, whose every victory motivated us to stay at the top. Maybe back then we didn’t value a Spanish Super Cup or a Copa del Rey as much as we should have done, but you have to celebrate and savour everything. It all matters. Fans eagerly awaited our matches to see us play, and that says it all.

Despite the exceptional and privileged life of being a professional footballer and playing for Barça though, I never felt different from others – or at least, I tried to live my life that way. From the outside, it might seem difficult to understand, but for me, it wasn’t hard to remain Andres. The closer you stay to the reality around you, the better. I know we’re sometimes seen as unapproachable, but I’ve always tried to be a normal person.

If you’re at Barça, there’s no better place to be. Since leaving my hometown of Fuentealbilla, I was convinced that it was the club where I wanted to stay. It became my home. My goal was always to succeed there and stay as long as possible, so in that sense, I was never tempted by the Premier League.

Early in my career, I’m told there was some talk about Rangers trying to sign me on loan, but I don’t remember it clearly. I’m not sure if they ever directly contacted my father or my agent. In any case, what I can say is that I never seriously considered leaving the club. Not at the beginning, nor later. I always had confidence that I would succeed at Barça and never entertained the idea of going on loan. I told myself, ‘Even if I don’t play much, I’m convinced I’ll end up playing’. A few minutes at Barça were worth more than anywhere else.

I would have liked to retire at Barça, but I had to make other decisions, and I think I did so at the right time, when I signed for Vissel Kobe in 2018. My last final for Barça, the Copa del Rey final against Sevilla, was unforgettable. I felt like I was flying on the pitch, everything just flowed, and I could end that wonderful chapter with a goal I’ll never forget. We won 5-0 – it was unbelievable!

Leaving wasn’t easy, but the club demands 300 per cent, and I couldn’t give that any more. Could I have stayed another year? Maybe, but I left with the memory of Iniesta as a Barça player in an incredible moment.

A few months ago, I announced my retirement at the age of 40, after a year playing for Emirates Club in the UAE Pro League. Which word defines how I feel about my career? Pride, in having worked hard until the very last training session. The rest is history: titles, defeats, good moments and bad ones. But what stands out to me is never giving up. I would have played until I was 90, but I’m happy to have fulfilled the dream of becoming a footballer.

For now, I plan to definitely stay in Dubai for 2025, then we’ll see. There’s family logistics to consider, like our children’s education, so we’ll try to manage it all. I’m also working on projects that allow me to keep learning. I don’t have time to get bored, even though everything is different. I still have the passion and enthusiasm to do what I do with commitment and dedication.

I’m doing a bit of everything – this is a new chapter of my life where I want to grow and explore different things. I have several businesses, like my agency Never Say Never (NSN) or Mikakus Barcelona, a sneaker company. I’m pursuing new interests with my team and we’ve invested in an exciting project at the Danish club Helsingor. I’ll try to absorb as much knowledge as possible over the coming months. I’m also enthusiastic about studying for my coaching licence in the future. Coaching motivates me a lot.

I know that many people expect me to coach Barça one day, but right now, I’m not thinking about that. For me, that’s a huge responsibility, especially since I’m just starting out. Of course it’s my home though, and hopefully one day I’ll return – we’ll see in what capacity and when. It would be beautiful. Guardiola, Xavi, and then Iniesta? Sounds good…

The Danish legend missed out on his country's only major tournament victory

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than 30 years on, Denmark's Euro 92 victory remains one of international football's most remarkable stories.

A team that had failed to qualify for the tournament would eventually go on to lift the trophy, having taken full advantage of Yugoslavia's ejection following the break-up of the country.

Goals from John Jensen and Kim Vilfort sealed a 2-0 win over Germany in the final, with the Danes claiming the stunning victory without one of their greatest-ever players, following Michael Laudrup's decision to walk away from international football two years earlier to focus on his Barcelona career.

The mercurial midfielder had been central to the rise of Danish Dynamite, the thrilling side that reached the semi-finals of Euro 84 before winning over the hearts and minds of so many at the 1986 World Cup. But his decision to prioritise club football meant he would miss Denmark's greatest triumph.

Speaking about the Danish side of the 1980s, Laudrup credited his manager and his team-mates' decision to ply their trade in Europe's best leagues.

"A lot of the players were playing for big clubs in Europe, at a time when not many foreign players were allowed in European leagues," Laudrup tells FourFourTwo. "We had a lot of individual quality. The arrival of Sepp Piontek as manager in 1979 was also pivotal – he fulfilled our potential. We went to the European Championship and beat Yugoslavia 5-0. We had a fantastic game against Belgium too, which we won 3-2 from 2-0 down. In the end, we only lost on penalties in the semi-final against Spain.

"At the 1986 World Cup, we beat Uruguay 6-1 and West Germany 2-0, but then went out against Spain in the last 16. We were 1-0 up, but a poor second half cost us and we lost 5-1. The big countries had tournament experience. We learned from that and could apply it in 1992 and 1998, where we achieved good results in the latter stages."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

And what about his decision to quit the Denmark team in 1990?

"In the second game of qualifying, we drew in Northern Ireland, then we lost at home against Yugoslavia, who had a fantastic team," Laudrup continues. "I realised they’d qualify, even if we beat them away. I was also in the early stages of my time at Barça, which was important to me, and the two teams played completely different football. I wasn’t really happy with the way we played in the national team, but it’s always the manager’s decision. Still, I thought, ‘With this style of play, I can never be the same as at Barcelona.’

"As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. People asked me if I wanted to go, but I didn’t want to join at the last moment, even though I could have. I felt it wouldn’t have been fair."

Laudrup would eventually return to the Danish national side in 1993.

"I’d won three league titles and the European Cup with Barça, and every time, they asked if I wanted to go back," he explains. "I’d achieved all the things I wanted with Barcelona, so I agreed. Unfortunately we lost a World Cup qualifier to Spain – the third time they got in our way, after beating us in 1984 and 1986. Spain has given me so much at personal and club level, then it’s curious how much it has taken away from me with the national team! But then we went to Euro 96 and the 1998 World Cup."

His 100th international cap came during the 1998 World Cup, with Laudrup calling time on his international career following their quarter-final defeat to Brazil.

"That was a great stage to retire on," he reflects. "After leaving Real Madrid, I went to Japan – I wanted to go somewhere I could still play, but also have a bit of freedom after being in Southern Europe since 1983. I thought maybe I should retire from the national team, but the coach asked me to continue. I realised that even though I liked life in Japan, I wanted to finish at a higher level. There was some interest from countries like Turkey and France – Marseille wanted me – but the Southern European passion was what I didn’t want any more! [Laughs]

"I joined Ajax – that team was incredible, with the De Boer brothers, Danny Blind, Edwin van der Sar and Jari Litmanen. We won the Double, so I continued with the national team, we qualified for the World Cup and lost in the quarter-finals to Brazil. We really challenged them and it was a great way to finish my career."

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1018. A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Lorenzo Valcanover is in the Division of Oncogenomics, Oncode Institute, the Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam 1066 CX, the Netherlands.

Reuven Agami is in the Division of Oncogenomics, Oncode Institute, the Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam 1066 CX, the Netherlands, and the Department of Genetics, Erasmus University Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

Identifying cellular properties that distinguish a cancer from healthy tissue is a crucial step for developing efficient treatments. One such characteristic is the ‘sloppy’ way in which some cancer cells implement translation — the process by which proteins are made from messenger RNA by protein complexes called ribosomes. This process can go awry. Writing in Nature, Wang et al.1 reveal a cancer-specific mechanism by which translation loses its normal ‘track’ of how it reads an mRNA sequence to encode the expected amino acids, resulting in a phenomenon called frameshifting. This generates proteins that have a distinct sequence of amino acids that are not usually made, and the authors show that this abnormality might be exploited for therapeutic purposes.

#1017. Emery endures heaviest European defeat as Villa manager to old foes Barcelona

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

Aston Villa make a mistake at the back and Lamine Yamal makes them pay inside 10 minutes ⚡ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/1IcWOPMJlt

At the heart of Barcelona’s victory was Lamine Yamal, their outstanding jewel from the academy. The 19-year-old became the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history, eclipsing the record of 13 he previously shared with Kylian Mbappé, with the opening goal.

Yamal was orchestrating everything from the pace of the match to the volume of the supporters, at one point imploring them to raise the noise in the first half with both arms aloft.

There was also another impressive performance from England international Anthony Gordon and Raphinha, who dedicated his two goals to the memory of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday.

With that tragedy fresh in the minds and the Nou Camp under construction, it was a peculiar atmosphere at times.

The defeat marked the end of Villa’s 100 per cent record in the competition, with a tough test away at Galatasaray up next before they host PSG in December. They remain high up in the table and have often displayed a propensity to bounce back quickly from defeats.

Emery said: “We are in a process and this was a very good test against a team like Barcelona. We are not at the level we want to achieve but there are a lot of experiences for us to take. Overall, we are competing fantastically in the Champions League and there is still work to do.

“Over the process we’ve had here, we have made mistakes but then overcame them. We accept this defeat but take a lot of information from it.”

Nine years have passed since Emery’s last visit in this competition and time has not proved a great healer.

Then in charge of PSG, Emery witnessed his team surrender a 4-0 first-leg lead to lose 6-5 on aggregate. Any matches where he is involved at the Nou Camp will revive memories of that remarkable comeback. He must have feared a repeat of more pain when Yamal, making his 37th Champions League appearance, rewarded Barcelona’s early pressure.

Villa’s defending needed to be as close to perfect as possible, but they were exposed after a poor error of judgment from Gomes. Under pressure from Barcelona’s attackers, Gomes panicked and played a blind pass into the path of Yamal, who bent his left-footed shot into the corner.

That mistake could have threatened to damage confidence but Villa did respond. Matty Cash’s half-volley from inside the penalty area was only a few inches wide, while Johan Manzambi side-footed wide of the goal after a quick break down the right from Nicolas Jackson.

With Andreas Christensen, Eric García, Xavi Espart and Jules Koundé all absent here, Barcelona’s defence did appear vulnerable. Jackson was targeting the flanks and having his more dangerous moments challenging their high line. Emery paced his technical area, imploring his players to remain focused.

Yet Barcelona’s forward three were always a threat and they increased their lead eight minutes into the second half. Raphinha was given too much room to turn in the penalty area and his shot took a heavy deflection off the heel of Pau Torres to find the bottom corner. Emery was furious, appearing to raise his fist in the air at another poor goal conceded.

Raphinha doubles Barcelona's lead with his 18th goal of the season! 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/NzFPYVzDuj

Barcelona added a third goal with Raphinha converting from close range after a sublime pass from João Cancelo.

Raphinha dedicated his goals to De Miguel, who died on Tuesday after sustaining serious injuries during a match the previous night. He said: “Tonight I don’t want to talk about football. I want to send a lot of strength to Jesus de Miguel’s family.

“May he rest in peace. In the end, this can happen to anyone. The truth is that it’s very tough. When we saw the news this morning, it was complicated. I’m incredibly shocked and sad. In the end, you go to play a match, and the same thing could happen to you. From myself, from the club, we want to send a lot of strength to his family.”

Villa did continue to fight for a consolation, with substitute Leon Goretzka heading against the post and their 3,000 travelling fans continued to sing in the rain after the final whistle.

This was the first encounter between the two clubs since the European Super Cup Final in January 1983, and yet another reminder of the upward trajectory under Emery.

"His numbers are staggering." 🤯 Joe Cole on Raphinha after he scored his 19th goal of the season in Barcelona's 3-0 win over Aston Villa ⭐ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOUq1QaYKE

“When you come to places like this, you need to start well and weather the storm, and we did not do this. When you play against teams like Barcelona, you do not get a second chance. There are lessons to be learnt. Our final pass let us down tonight. Barcelona made the right decisions at the right times. The manager spoke about being clinical in important moments in the game. Unai Emery’s side will be relieved that they took a maximum nine points from their opening three games as their fixtures in this competition are getting a lot harder. Unai Emery has managed more than 1,100 matches but will never forget the drama of “La Remontada” as he returns to the scene on Tuesday night.

Emery is back at the Nou Camp in the Champions League for the first time since one of the most epic games in the history of the competition. While in charge of Paris St-Germain nine years ago, Emery took his team to Barcelona with a 4-0 lead from the round-of-16 first leg. Yet he was left stunned as Barcelona recovered to win the rematch 6-1, with three goals in the final seven minutes and the winner proving hugely controversial.

Sergi Roberto’s goal five minutes into added time caused a massive backlash as PSG claimed it was offside, with Emery claiming on Monday that the match showed that VAR was “necessary”.

No such luck, however, and it is pretty torrential at the moment. Football updates to follow.

Aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

#1016. Jamie Carragher discusses his evolution from pitch to studio

The former Liverpool defender has been a Sky Sports regular for more than a decade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Immediately after hanging up his boots, Jamie Carragher moved into the media world, with Sky Sports signing up the former Liverpool and England defender at the start of the 2013/14 season.

Over the past 13 years, Carragher has become of the most recognisable and distinct voices in football broadcasting, whether that was sparring with Gary Neville on Monday Night Football back in the day, or showing his lighter side on shows such as Stick to Football.

But how does he assess his own evolution from player to pundit? And how does he compare himself with his former on-pitch rival Neville?

“There are parts of understanding football where Gary’s on a completely different level to me – his understanding of how the leagues work, or the EFL,” Carragher tells FourFourTwo, referencing Neville’s role as co-owner of League Two club Salford City.

“He’s in meetings because he’s an owner, and he had a really good take on things like Covid, when there was no football going on, and also things like a football regulator and how deals are done, whereas I don’t. He’s an authority on subjects like that. And he’s also the authority on winning the Premier League – I have to accept that.”

For Carragher, research, preparation and tactical insight is where he excels in front of camera – even if on a show such as Stick to Football, that can get overshadowed by a witty one-liner from someone else on the panel. “It can be a little frustrating,” Carragher smiles.

“But that’s the nature of the show. If I make a point, then someone comes out with, ‘It’s just 11 vs 11, it’s just 22 men kicking the ball around’, you can think, ‘What’s f**king the point in anything!’”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For Carragher, though, it’s this detail and alternative ways of analysing the game that keeps him engaged.

“But everybody sees the game in a different way, and I love the details – that’s what gets my juices flowing,” he continues. “Finding something or a bit of analysis that no one else has seen.

“A lot of the time there are these myths in football, about things that happened years ago, but when you actually look at the detail, they didn’t f**king happen!”

Given his love for detail, how does Carragher view this stage of his career in football, compared to his playing days? “I was a very good player, but I’m a great pundit,” he jokes.

“Modest!” laughs Neville, sat beside him. “As for me, I always said that on my tombstone, it would say ‘Six out of 10’. I like the idea of being consistent.

“I don’t think I’m better as a pundit or player, I think I’m consistent.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1015. Germany's Merz says erosion of global order means middle powers in Europe and Asia must be more assertive

During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the top stories in Germany on Tuesday, October 27, 2026:

Don't want to miss our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Thank you for joining our coverage of German news on Tuesday.

We look forward to bringing you the latest again on Wednesday in a fresh blog.

On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.

"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."

Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.

Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.

Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."

"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind.

"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."

Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.

Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.

Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.

A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.

Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.

His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.

The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.

The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.

German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has cut its forecast for 2026, with difficult market conditions in China and higher fourth-quarter cost expectations set to negatively impact profits, the company said on Tuesday.

Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.

The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.

Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.

Mercedes currently expects an adjusted car profit margin of 2% to 3% in 2026, compared to the 3% to 5% in the previous guidance.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Like many German automakers, Mercedes has faced weak sales in China. German carmakers have struggled in the world's largest car market with sluggish demand and increased competition from local manufacturers.

Mercedes vehicle deliveries in China — last year already at their lowest level since 2016 — fell a further 29% in the nine months to the end of September.

Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.

Before interest and tax, Mercedes posted an operating profit of €1.77 billion — more than double the €750 million recorded a year earlier, according to the preliminary figures. But last year's stats were significantly impacted by one-time expenses, especially related to job cuts and legal disputes.

Adjusted for one-off items, the operating profit margin in the passenger car business stood at 2.5%, down on the 4.8% recorded a year earlier.

The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.

Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.

Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.

Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.

BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.

The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.

The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.

As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.
