Arsenal full-back Riccardo Calafiori could leave the club in a shock move.

That's according to a new report, which claims that the champions have to be wary that their superstar Italian could be about to depart North London after three years.

Calafiori has been excellent for Arsenal this season – but with the star's contract reaching the two-year mark next summer, the Gunners might have to consider cashing in if they can't extend.

The Gunners won their first fixture at Anfield in 14 years yesterday, with Calafiori a member of the back four that kept yet another clean sheet in the Premier League to go top of the table.

The 24-year-old has arguably been the North Londoners' player of the season thus far, chipping in with goals and assists in attack, while remaining a part of the most impressive back four on the continent.

This has alerted Real Madrid, who are weighing up a move for the defender, as per TEAMtalk.

Los Blancos signed Marc Cucurella over the summer to bolster their options at left-back, but with Calafiori able to play centrally, Bernabeu boss Jose Mourinho is said to value the Arsenal man's versatility, considering him a “dream” signing and Real “enquiring” about a move, after playing the star nine times during his time as Roma manager.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that Real were in the race for the Italian when he eventually left Bologna for North London in 2024, with Arsenal rushing to complete the signing, believing that it was a significant upgrade in that area of the pitch.

But while Calafiori has unlocked a new dimension to manager Mikel Arteta's attack when he's been fit, his contract ticking down – with an expiry in 2029 – may represent an opportunity to sell the star.

FourFourTwo understands that the champions plan to address his extension along with the likes of Martin Odegaard, Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice, though with Calafiori having suffered a number of injuries during his time in English football, Arsenal may have to weigh up whether an attractive bid – and Calafiori's own interest in Real – makes a sale appealing.

Calafiori suffered a potentially career-ending knee injury as a teenager, only to bounce back impressively and rebuild his career via a spell in Switzerland.

Since moving to the Premier League, however, the Rome-born star has suffered eight separate injuries, missing 13 matches in all competitions after Christmas last season, and seeing Piero Hincapie start the Champions League final ahead of him.

Calafiori is worth €65 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel to Slavia Prague this week as Champions League action continues this week.

#991. Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny

Senegal is hosting Africa's first Youth Olympics, with 2,700 young athletes competing in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. The Games bring pride and hope, but also questions over cost, rights and legacy.

On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports.

Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future.

"I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW.

"I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 Youth Games in Senegal will also be a first beyond the history it is making in Africa.

"Of the 2,700 athletes who will be competing in Dakar, there will be a 50-50 split between men and women," Olivia Nloga, Chief Brand Promotion Officer on the organizing committee, told DW.

"But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists."

Several sports are also making their debut at the Youth Olympic Games, such as five-a-side baseball, kung fu and the Senegalese specialty of beach wrestling. There's also a refugee team at the Youth Olympic Games for the first time.

"As I said earlier, the Youth Olympic Games aren't just about sports, and they aren't just about infrastructure," said Nloga.

"For us, it was also important to use this time to build on and reinforce the idea that these Games in Senegal are a celebration for the people. We did this by investing in culture—for example, through a fashion show and a program called Yi-sol, which is a mural project on the city's walls."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other projects designed to celebrate the people include music, and a local student designed the mascot. The biggest focus of all though, is on creating sustainability for the young people of Senegal.

"We did so through a program that is very important to us – one that is close to our hearts, namely, the Olympic Civic and Sports Certificate," Nloga said.

"We traveled to schools throughout Senegal and worked with more than 1,000 instructors to reach and make an impact on more than one million young Senegalese children who, during this hiatus, were exposed to and educated about the values of the Olympic Movement."

With recent flooding in the country, there were concerns that infrastructure would have been affected, but Nloga insisted that flood risk had long been in the planning.

"The prime minister held an interdepartmental meeting during which he established a task force to ensure that the necessary arrangements and follow-up measures are put in place to safeguard both the competition venues and the accommodation sites."

With Formula 1 confirming its return to Africa earlier in October, global sport is slowly becoming a more regular event in Africa. As a result though, there have been questions asked about the legacy of such events.

Many in Senegal concerned by the high cost of living and unemployment will see these Games as an unnecessary expense. For the Senegalese authorities though, they are an opportunity for long-term investment in the country's young people as well as infrastructure. There is also the hope that this will make Dakar a major tourist destination.

There was further criticism of the Games being in Senegal from Human Rights Watch (HRW), with the NGO calling on the Senegalese authorities to change their stance on the LGBTQ+ community.

"You are welcoming all of the world. It shouldn't be 'you are welcome to our country, except this, except that,'" Larissa Kojoue from HRW told DW.

"Anti-LGBT legislation and that crackdown that is going on, they contradict the Olympic movement, the Olympic Charter, and also various human rights convention that the country has signed."

Earlier this year, Senegal President Bassirou Diomaye Faye signed into law new legislation on same-sex relations that have proved contentious abroad despite broad political support within the majority Muslim country's parliament. Several human rights groups had voiced concerns about the bill, including warning that it would dissuade people at risk of illnesses like HIV/AIDS from seeking help.

The Games were set to see the return of Russians to Olympic competition under their own colours after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted their suspension in July.

However, the Russian Athletics Federation (RusAF) released a statement the day before the opening ceremony saying the reported 13 athletes (and 10 coaches) had been exluded from the competition. They demanded an explanation and asked for the decision to be reconsidered.

"The IOC-endorsed position was clear in its direction: young athletes holding Russian or Belarusian passports should no longer be restricted from international youth competitions. That principle should apply to Dakar 2026," read the statement.

Despite the IOC's ruling, each federation can still decide whether to authorize Russian participation. World Athletics, has clearly upheld their ban, while swimming and judo have allowed Russian athletes back.

"This has enabled World Athletics to pursue its own exclusory agenda in the face of clear and just directions from the IOC. This activism is only detrimental to youth sports, with the result being that Russian young athletes will be denied the opportunity to compete at these Games."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the various concerns, there is an overriding hope that the Games will be prove beneficial for all involved.

"What makes the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar special is that they are also rooted in Senegal's extremely strong sporting culture," Nloga said.

"Every evening, when you take a stroll along the Corniche in Dakar, you're struck by the number of people you see exercising, regardless of their age or physical condition. What we'll be offering during these Olympic Games is also an immersion into Senegalese life – into the way sports are just as much a part of Senegalese identity."

This article was updated on October 30, 2026 to reflect the change in situation for Russian athletes at the Games.

Sira Thierij conducted interviews for this article. Edited by: Chuck Penfold

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is growing in belief. Following this 2-1 victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held onto long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing of his players. So smooth at first, Arsenal then became remarkably open as the game wore on. Slavia deserve credit for that, but there is no doubt that Arteta’s side became complacent. They were perhaps a little fortunate not to be punished for it.

Wiktor Nowak’s 90th-minute goal was hard-earned by the Czech side, who had found a way to rattle the Arsenal defence with long balls and direct runs. It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and there were plenty of reasons for them to feel confident upon their return here.

Among those reasons was Slavia’s poor form in Europe’s premier competition. The Czech side came into the match on a run of 22 games without victory in the Champions League, and in the knowledge that one more game without a win would equal the European Cup record.

To make matters worse for the home side, they recently banished their star striker from the club due to a series of disciplinary failings. Tomas Chory, Slavia’s top scorer for the past two seasons, has been chucked out of the team after showing his middle finger to the referee in a recent game. This sort of sanction would have earned Arteta’s nod of approval, no doubt, but it probably did not increase Slavia’s chances of hurting the Premier League champions.

Overall, then, this was always unlikely to be the most challenging contest of Arsenal’s European campaign. Arteta being Arteta, though, he still picked many of his favourites. There was no rest for Declan Rice, Ezri Konsa or Gabriel Magalhaes, who all started in the Prague chill.

As was to be expected, Arsenal were dominant from the start. Each member of the front three looked dangerous, with Madueke, Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze all winning their individual battles with their opponents.

The opening goal arrived after just nine minutes, when Gyokeres hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

Madueke and Ben White then combine well, but Eze cannot quite let fly from a central position. The Arsenal left-winger drifting across the line to receive the ball in that move.

Quite an industrious start from the home team, trying to close Arsenal down, but Merino and Zubimendi combined well in a tight space to help Arsenal move forward. The flag goes up against Ben White for offside, possibly mistakenly.

At the other end Sturm caused Konsa a problem, but the Arsenal defender recovered well and the goal kick decision was in his favour too, much to the annoyance of the home crowd.

Arsenal also paid their respects at Colney to the 30-year-old Spanish player who died after a collision with the Andorra’s goalkeeper.

Declan Rice is wearing the captain’s armband and leads Arsenal out at a smoky Fortuna Arena. Slavia Prague are celebrating their 144th birthday, and marked the occasion with a choir and classical music.

Real Madrid struck late to drag themselves out of jail at AEK Athens and join PSG on maximum points from four games. Arsenal cannot catch those two sides tonight, but they do host Real next month.

Slavia are without their top scorer from the last two seasons, Tomas Chory, for rather unusual reasons. Good evening from a chilly Prague, where Arsenal are looking for a repeat of the 3-0 victory they secured here exactly one year ago. It’s a remarkable coincidence that Mikel Arteta’s team have travelled to face Slavia Prague on November 4th in back-to-back years.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

Under-fire Manchester United boss Michael Carrick has made a remarkably candid admission regarding his Old Trafford future

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Carrick appears to have accepted that his tenure at Old Trafford could soon be brought to an abrupt end.

Speaking ahead of Man United’s next game, a Champions League showdown with AS Roma, Carrick was fatalistic in tone when questioned about the mounting speculation surrounding his position.

Rather than offering standard managerial press conference fare of defiance in the face of public scrutiny, the 45-year-old openly acknowledged the reality of his situation.

"I can’t look into the future, I don’t know what’s gonna happen,” Carrick admitted, in quotes via The Athletic. “I am really looking forward to the game tomorrow, you might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had. Whatever happens will happen after that, whatever direction it goes in.”

The mood around the club has turned following a run of just two wins in nine matches across all competitions. A five-game winless streak, an early Carabao Cup exit, and a return of seven points from their opening nine Premier League fixtures has left Man United drastically off the pace.

Recent domestic displays, which include failing to capitalise against 10 men versus Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur, were compounded by a dispiriting Champions League defeat away to Atletico Madrid, after which Lisandro Martinez spoke out against the club hierarchy.

Martinez broke rank to deliver a stinging critique of the club's summer recruitment, reportedly sparking an argument with a teammate on the flight back to Manchester. With a dressing room unravelling and Carrick's gentler approach failing to provoke a response, the popular view is that the club's faith in his faculties to turn things around has plummeted.

To some, his latest quotes indicate a recognition that the writing is on the wall, and with the November international break coming up, that could be the opportune time for the club to sever ties with the former interim head coach.

Old Trafford is likely to have a new first-team manager before long - national outlets have already linked Brighton’s Fabian Hurzeler alongside more experienced coaches Antonio Conte and Unai Emery.

At a club the size of Manchester United, once a manager hums 'que sera, sera', the inevitable is rarely far behind.

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The 16-year-old forward has not trained at Manchester United’s Carrington base since falling out with the club over his development

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Real Madrid are closing in on the signing of Manchester United wonderkid JJ Gabriel in a major blow to the Old Trafford club.

Gabriel, who turned 16 last month, told United he wanted to leave in September and his representatives have been in contact with the biggest clubs in Europe, including Bayern Munich and Barcelona.

Multiple reports on Wednesday suggested Gabriel had chosen Madrid and agreed personal terms, and although there have been no club-to-club talks, he is set to move to the Spanish capital in January. He is thought to have an EU passport, enabling him to make the switch at such a young age, while United would be due compensation for the loss of a homegrown young player.

Gabriel is registered to United’s academy until the end of the season, but has not trained since falling out with the Old Trafford hierarchy over his development amid disagreement over the club’s cautious approach to his exposure at a young age.

Gabriel, whose father is the former Irish international Joe O'Cearuill, was barely used in pre-season and his family were unhappy with the then 15-year-old’s lack of involvement in first-team duties, as well as his exclusion from Champions League games this season.

Speaking after the rift emerged in September, United manager Michael Carrick said: “We’ve got to be really careful of the whole situation. He’s a young boy ... from a club point of view, looking after our younger players – their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure – we’ve got to be really conscious of that in this situation.”

The youngster, who primarily plays as a left winger or a No 10, grew up in London and spent stints at numerous top academies, including Chelsea, Arsenal, West Ham and Queens Park Rangers.

He garnered fame aged just eight, showing off his skills in a viral YouTube video which earned him the nickname “Kid Messi”.

Gabriel went on to join United’s youth setup at the age of 11, where he soon became regarded as one of the club’s brightest prospects.

He became the youngest winner of the club’s Jimmy Murphy Young Player of the Year award last season after scoring more than 20 goals for the United’s Under-18 side. Gabriel’s goalscoring exploits also saw him named the Under-18 Premier League Player of the Season.

The forward’s real name is Joseph O’Cearuill but he goes under the name JJ Gabriel in football, reportedly for commercial reasons.

This kind of nonsense usually only surfaces around the international break.

An incredible stat, however, has re-emerged concerning Manchester City goalkeeper Ronald Waterreus (remember him?) and his opposite number Nick Colgan (remember him? No?) from around 20 years ago that's sure to blow your mind.

And after digging, it gets even stranger.

Back in 2004/05, only two matches across the entirety of Great Britain in all competitions ended 7-1 – which is not that strange, given that it's an unusual scoreline.

The first came when Man City smashed Barnsley in the League Cup in September, with Waterreus between the sticks for the Citizens and Colgan conceding those seven goals for the Tykes.

The other match that ended with that scoreline, you ask? Well, obviously it was another League Cup game – this time north of the border – between Rangers and Dundee United.

The goalkeepers in that match, you ask? Take a wild guess.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That's right: David James' back-up, Waterreus, had moved to the Gers in search of more game time in January, while Colgan joined United on loan in January 2005.

But the oddness doesn't end there: both matches were club debuts for Waterreus.

The symmetry is startling, especially when you consider that the Dutchman played just a handful of times at City, while Colgan made just two appearances during that stint in Scottish football.

With the fact making its way back onto social media recently, it's probably time to remind everyone of just how much of an incredible coincidence it really is.

So much so, that it featured on a list of extraordinary football facts we published last year…

Consistent team selection and simpler patterns should be the order of the day at Stamford Bridge this season, but Alonso doesn't seem to be offering that yet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The billions spent on young players and the constant churn for accountancy tricks, the erratic form and the bottom-half finishes: Chelsea are engulfed in an identity crisis of their own making and everybody knows Xabi Alonso needs a transitional year to sort this mess out.

What’s needed is stability, order, calm; qualities Chelsea’s owners carelessly abandoned across the first four years of their tech bro, move-fast-and-break-things philosophy. The decision to hire Alonso as ‘manager’ and not ‘head coach’ - and to allow over-30s into the training ground - tells us they have learnt their lesson.

But does Alonso, rocking up in this new and better environment, appreciate the chaos that came before him, that still hums in the background at Stamford Bridge? Judging by the instability, disorder, and erratic tactical setups this season, the answer is no. Alonso is a world-class coach, but he appears to be overthinking his tactics, which is the last thing such a tangled-up squad needs.

In nine Premier League matches, Alonso has used six different combinations in defence and five different combinations of a two-man midfield. As we have highlighted before, he made the strange decision to trial a Henderson-Barco pivot in the defeat at Brentford, and then he got found out by an even stranger strikerless 4-4-2 in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham.

On Saturday, the tactical overthinking was a little harder to spot, but, again, complexity was unnecessarily introduced to a fixture against a Manchester United team waiting to be beaten. Chelsea were a shambles in the first half thanks to a strange use of Cole Palmer that scrambled brains in the middle of the park. When Alonso corrected his error with a far more normal 4-2-3-1 in the second half, Chelsea strode to victory.

In that chaotic end-to-end first half, Chelsea consistently lost possession in the middle of the park (leading to quick United transitions, then quick Chelsea counters back the other way, hence the carnage) because Palmer’s position meant the passing lanes weren’t open. Chelsea, lacking depth (or ‘verticality’), could not pass forward in an orderly fashion and therefore could not maintain a solid shape:

In the second half, Alonso normalised things by playing Palmer higher and suddenly Manchester United couldn’t cope with the passes through the lines.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Even the crucial opener was indirectly affected by this, with Manchester United players seemingly distracted away from Morgan Rogers by Palmer’s lurking presence.

There is a clear lesson here for Alonso: his players – young, new to the club, recovering from the tornado that was 2025/26 – need a firm hand on the tiller; consistent team selection, simple patterns, and the opportunity to discover what it means to play for a normal club.

In other words, these players have spent enough time charging around in circles. They need to be taught how to walk before they can run.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

#984. Can the power of Old Trafford and vibes save Michael Carrick at Man United?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United’s remarkable comeback to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League earned Carrick a stay of execution and now, he must try to take advantage

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United had spent some of Tuesday night hovering just above the dotted line, 24th in a 36-team group, with Azeri champions Sabah 25th and with a game in hand on them. There are ample indications these days of how the mighty have fallen.

With a triple Champions League finalist in the technical area, United were below Bodo/Glimt in the virtual standings, at risk of being leapfrogged a day later by Sabah and AEK Athens. There have been plenty of historic lows at Old Trafford of late, but at least even they cannot come 24th, let alone any lower, in the Premier League.

A spectacular comeback later and Old Trafford was engulfed by euphoria. A turnaround was powered by bricks and mortar; or the people in that famous old ground because of them, of the past deeds they had witnessed there. “I don’t like to keep talking to the lads about what this place can do in history and what’s gone before them too much, but it’s there,” said Carrick.

The accusation is that United are trapped by their past, spending too long talking about it and even longer hearing their former greats turned podcasters discussing it, flailing when they appoint their ex-players as managers in bids to recreate it, blinded to the evidence that the footballing world has changed.

In their time of need, Manchester United won because they were Manchester United, and occasionally still can be. They beat Roma because of their ground which, in an inconvenient detail, co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe wants to replace with a new stadium in what United have called a sanity project, in part because many another feel it reeks of vanity.

It hardly feels a failsafe footballing formula for an immediate renaissance, and not merely because they already play half of their games at grounds not called Old Trafford.

Sir Alex Ferguson, the architect of many a comeback, was watching and the temptation at such times is to wonder if this was Carrick’s Mark Robins moment, the transformative game that alters the direction of a reign, a club, an entire era.

The prosaic answer is: probably not. United have been here before. Even in a malaise that has occupied much of the last 13 years, there have been some glorious European evenings. David Moyes grasped at a lifeline when United, 2-0 down after the first leg, beat Olympiakos 3-0. He lasted barely a month longer.

With Carrick on his coaching staff, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer saw his United go 2-0 down to a Gian Piero Gasperini side, recover to defeat Atalanta 3-2 and, like Moyes, extend his tenure, but only for a few weeks. Ruben Amorim had his own crazy comeback: from 4-2 down against 10-man Lyon to 5-4 winners. He still lost the Europa League final. It was the beginning of the end.

Carrick has seemed to face the end; at least twice, with his innate calmness. He was given a stay of execution after the 3-0 home shellacking by Bournemouth, in part because sporting director Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada seemingly did not know what to do next. After Saturday’s loss at Chelsea, it felt likely Carrick would go in the international break. Now it feels plausible he is still in charge after it.

And yet it is also true that, until Matheus Cunha intervened against Roma, United were on course to go 10 games without a win in the same season for the first time since Carrick was born. It is also true that United could be bottom of the Premier League by the time they kick off against Aston Villa on Sunday, and then for the international break, and then for a trip to Liverpool. Theirs has been the form of a team in a relegation battle.

That United’s players, flawed as the squad is, have been underachieving was illustrated in the frenetic final 35 minutes against Roma. They ended up overwhelming the side third in Serie A. After the capitulations to Como and Bournemouth, there were crucial signs they have not given up on Carrick. There had been some indications in the first half at Chelsea, before their self-destructive streak surfaced again.

Perhaps it was telling that there were boos for Lisandro Martinez, who was sent off at Stamford Bridge, when he came on against Roma. United’s players were cheered at the end, but their relationship with the crowd is still fragile. Bruno Fernandes took his own step towards redemption; and yet, after the last two months, do the United faithful still trust their team?

The most positive comments about them have tended to come from Carrick; belatedly, he was repaid for a little of his faith. Yet issues do not just remain: some have been compounded. The left half of United’s defence has been disastrous this season; Martinez, who has been dreadful, is suspended on Sunday but Ayden Heaven was awful on Tuesday. Midfield has been a permanent problem and Carlos Baleba, the most mobile of the four options, is now injured.

They face objectively better teams now in Villa and Liverpool. They lost their next game after Lyon and Atalanta, suggesting they were one-offs, wins that delayed sackings rather than altering the trajectory of a tenure. Maybe Carrick will carry momentum and energy into the Villa game.

The strategy might be to rely on Old Trafford and on vibes. It is scarcely a perfect recipe but, if only for one night, it worked.

#983. Russia in Africa: What is Putin hoping to achieve?

Following its invasion of Ukraine and the resulting rift with the West, Russia has declared that it intends to make a "historic return" to Africa. What have we seen of this so far?

The conflict with the West sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine  prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek support from other parts of the world. Africa has become a focus, with foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visiting the continent increasingly often.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has described it as a "historic return," and declared no one and nothing could be compared to what Russia did for Africa in the 20th century.

A Russia-Africa summit has been held in Russia at roughly three-year intervals since 2019. The third takes place in Moscow on October 28 and 29. The program focusses on economic cooperation. Other topics range from politics and security to science and culture. But Russia is actively working with only a few African countries, mainly in the north of the continent, and this is reflected in the trade figures.

"South Africa is still Africa's largest national economy, but its volume of trade with Russia is small, far less than with Egypt and Algeria," says Ivan Klyszcz from the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn, Estonia.

"Egypt and Algeria in particular are key partners for Russia. Egypt plays an important role in this regard. Russian diplomats and business representatives are trying to extend relationships with other countries, especially Tanzania and Ethiopia, but with no appreciable success so far."

Egypt is the second-largest economy in Africa, and the bilateral volume of trade with Russia has more than doubled since 2021; in 2025, according to Russia's Federal Customs Service, it was $10.5 billion (€9.4 billion). Consignments of Russian grain are the main drivers, followed by products of the metal industry. Egypt's exports to Russia are primarily fruit and vegetables.

There are investment projects, too. Russia is building a big nuclear power plant in the Egyptian region of El-Dabaa on the Mediterranean coast. Construction is being financed by a Russian loan of 25 billion US dollars, which covers around 85% of the costs.

Egypt is one of the few African countries with which Russia enjoys stable business relationships, as well as having extensive experience of cooperation, says Nikita Smagin, an expert on Russian policy in the Middle East. "In the long term, Egypt could become Moscow's gateway to Africa and to other markets," he says. "But Cairo is pursuing its own interests. It would be too optimistic to hope that Egypt is lending its support purely out of political solidarity."

According to the Russian customs service, around 39% of Russian–African trade in 2025 was with Egypt, and total sales between Russia and all 54 countries of the African continent came to around 27 billion US dollars. Africa's share of Russia's foreign trade is therefore very small (3.9% in 2025), and not at all commensurate with the attention Moscow is devoting to its relations with African countries.

Russia is not a significant trading partner for Africa, either. The most important partner for African countries is the European Union. In 2025, the volume of trade with the EU came to around 385 billion US dollars. African countries' statistics also show that other partners were well ahead of Russia. The volume of trade with China was in excess of 348 billion US dollars in 2025; with the United States it was almost 105 billion, and 103 billion with India.

Fidel Owusu, a Ghanaian expert with Geopolitical Intelligence Services (GIS) in Liechtenstein, comments that Russia's economic presence in Africa has not been as significant as that of China, the United States, India, or other traditional powers like France and Britain. "If you look at the volume of trade and the kind of investment," he says, "in recent times, some middle powers such as Turkey and the UAW are doing far better than Russia."

Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst with Control Risks, a global risk and strategic intelligence consultancy in Senegal, observes: "Western countries continue to dominate in strategically important areas such as raw material extraction, finance, and the energy sector, even if their political presence in the region is declining." According to her, "Russia will compete more intensively for access to critical mineral resources and energy projects. We see this with lithium projects in Mali as well as with nuclear power initiatives across the continent."

Russia's presence in Africa is more obvious in the military sector than in the fields of trade and investment. Starting with the arrival of the Wagner Group, Russian mercenaries have been supporting African regimes, particularly those of the unstable countries in the Sahel region. In exchange, their associated subsidiaries are granted access to raw materials. Following the death of the Wagner Group leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin, most of these operations were taken over by the Africa Corps, a paramilitary group set up and controlled by Russia's defense ministry.

According to the Congressional Research Service, the think tank of the US Congress, the largest Russian military contingents, each comprising several thousand men, are in the Central African Republic, Mali, and Libya. The Africa Corps is also keen to extend its presence in Burkina Faso and Niger. Russian mercenaries have also been spotted in Equatorial Guinea.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Irina Filatova from the University of Cape Town stresses that there are several reasons why it's important for Russia to maintain a military presence in Africa. "The countries have sizeable deposits of minerals such as gold and uranium. Through them, it's possible to exert influence over Europe's southern borders, including in matters of migration and regional security. With regard to Libya, the country is an important logistical hub for connections with the Sahel and central Africa. Goods can easily be supplied via Libya to countries without access to the sea," Filatova says.

Ultimately, Russia is still one of the biggest suppliers of arms to African countries, even though Russian exports have fallen over the course of the war in Ukraine. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates Moscow's share of the African market for the years 2021–2025 at 15%, which puts it in third place behind the United States (19%) and China (17%). Between 2020 and 2024, its share was even higher: It was in first place with 21%, followed by China with 18%, and the US with 16%.

Ivan Klyszcz from the ICDS says that while Russia is not a significant economic partner for Africa, the fact that it supplies food and fertilizer and has a military presence in some countries means that Moscow's influence in Africa is far greater than is suggested by the volume of trade and investment alone.

"I believe Russia sees the diplomatic weight of Africa," says Fidel Owusu. "When I talk of diplomatic weight, I mean numbers – the continent has the largest number of countries. Russia wants that kind of support in the UN General Assembly whenever votes are cast. In recent times it has done better than in earlier votes."

In recent years, Russia has been positioning itself on the international stage as representing the interests of the Global South.

"We want to work with Africa, we are working with Africa and we will continue to do so. But our aim is not, as it was for the colonial powers, to make money or steal something from Africa, but to develop together," Russian president Vladimir Putin said recently at a conference of the Moscow-based Valdai Discussion Club.

References to the colonial past appeal to some countries but not others, says Irina Filatova. "Africa is not a country, it's a continent. There are differences in the perception of Russia, as well as in the way Russia positions itself. Also, the views of the political elites are often substantially different from those of ordinary citizens. In South Africa, for instance, the Russian narrative is received very positively. An anti-colonial agenda is also popular in other countries, but it isn't necessarily associated with Russia."

Antonio Cascais contributed to this report. It was originally written in Russian.

#980. Tennis legend Rafael Nadal joins Real Madrid board

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Rafael Nadal won 22 grand slam titles in his tennis career before retiring in 2024

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Real Madrid have added Rafael Nadal to their board of directors.

The tennis star's appointment was agreed at a club board meeting on Wednesday. The board will now ask the general assembly of delegate members to ratify Nadal as a new member of the board.

Nadal retired from tennis in 2024 after a career that brought him 22 grand slam singles titles. Fourteen of those came at the French Open, a record at the tournament.

A club statement described Nadal as “one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world”.

The statement added: “For Real Madrid and for all Madridismo it is a great pride that a figure of his sporting and human dimension, a benchmark in Spanish and world sport, becomes part of our board of directors and contributes, from this responsibility, to the present and future of our club.”

Real's statement continued: "With his extraordinary track record, with 92 individual titles, including 22 grand slams, two Olympic gold medals, five Davis Cups with Spain and number one in the world ranking, Rafael Nadal has starred in a legendary sporting career.

"But his figure represents much more than his successes: his talent, his spirit of permanent improvement, his capacity for sacrifice, his competitiveness, his humility, his respect for rivals and his team-mates, and his commitment to solidarity make him an example on and off the courts.

“All these values are part of Real Madrid’s identity and Rafael Nadal has represented and defended them throughout his sporting life, becoming a reference for millions of people around the world.”

Nadal has spoken in previous interviews about his love of Real Madrid since childhood. That affection has persisted despite his uncle Miguel Angel Nadal having played for their bitter rivals Barcelona.

He has held honorary membership of Real for years and has been a regular at matches at the Bernabeu. Nadal was a guest of honour at the 2022 Champions League final in Paris, when Real won their 14th Champions League title.

Responding to the appointment, Nadal wrote on X: "I want to thank President Florentino Pérez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of @realmadrid.

“I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can.”

#979. Man City have a striker who will not be stopped and a defence that cannot be trusted

This thrilling victory for Manchester City followed a familiar pattern this season: defensive errors and poor goalkeeping followed by Erling Haaland saving the day.

“How can you stop Haaland?” read the headline in the local Volkszeitung newspaper on the morning of this Champions League clash. The answer is that has been impossible for RB Leipzig when they have faced the Norwegian.

He has now scored 13 goals against them in nine matches, the most he has scored against a single team during his career. Enzo Maresca gave him the armband here and his winning goal masked more worries for the City head coach in his backline.

After being gifted the lead through Castello Lukeba’s own goal, Gianluigi Donnarumma was exposed at his near post by Ridle Baku’s cheeky finish when the City goalkeeper was positioned for a cross.

Maresca was not happy either with Antonio Nusa finding a second equaliser for Leipzig after Enzo Fernández had headed City back in front.

Haaland had to wait patiently for his chance. He had only three touches of the ball in the first half but slid in for the winner when Elliot Anderson broke forward.

This was a victory to bounce back from losing in the Premier League at the weekend, but the question will be how can City mount a title challenge with such a brittle defence? Champions League winners do not leave themselves open at the back like this, and City have now gone seven without a clean sheet.

It’s the most I’ve scored against one club [13] but I’ve played so many times against them. Leipzig are a good team. [Anderson] has been amazing, an amazing start to his City career. That’s what you expect to be honest. You have to come straight in and perform, It’s not easy. You need time to adapt, time to get to know your new team-mates and coach, which is not easy even for us, and he’s been very impressive. Respect!

Thirteen touches I had today, you say? It’s not the most but what is important is that I help the team to win and I managed to do that today. So I am super happy.

In the end we need to step up a little bit. When we went 1-0 up we should have pushed for the second more and then hopefully the third. That’s what we have to work at. Keep the ball, when to keep it when to go. Working together both offensively and defensively but that’s the good part there’s always a chance to get better. There’s always a new game and our next chance will be in three days.

You can look at [keeping focused to make the right runs despite the lack of touches] in different ways – either 100 minutes is a long time to stay concentrated or 100 minutes is not that long to stay concentrated. I look at it like the second option.

Haaland hits the post with a right-foot shot from an offside position after either jumping the gun or, more likely, Cherki delaying the pass too long.

Foden traps Banzuzi’s defensive header with his right to shift it on to his left then bends a shot that goes whistling past the left post.

Anderson snaps into the press and opens the door down the right for Ndiaye who can’t get away from Raum.

Baku is booked for scything down O’Reilly who had laid the ball off long before Baku dived in.

Gruda butchers a very good chance on the right of the City box after Fernandez and Cherki are caught upfield and leave Anderson minding the shop all alone. Baku, coming round Gruda, was screaming for the lay-up to shoot but Gruda took it on himself and scuffed it tamely wide.

Leipzig are guilty of overelaboration in and around the City box. Too many tricks and flicks, not enough shots and crosses. Haaland is giving his team-mates some jip for not reading his runs.

Cherki pings a pass out to Enzo on the right and he slips as he tries to cross, his momentum as he fell forcing the cross deeper than he had planned and it sails beyond a visibly frustrated Haaland who keeps making good runs but has yet to be found.

City are dicing with danger by letting Nusa run at them from positions on both wings and through the middle. They manage to stop him threading ir flicking passes through to Romulo twice in the space of 30 seconds but it would be less stressful to cut it off at source further away from their goal.

City can’t hang on to the ball in high areas, yielding possession too cheaply and Leipzig swarm forward down the right with City scrambling back. Khusanov, under pressure from Romulo, squeezes a pass that deflects off him and goes out for a City throw-in.

The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

#978. EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers

In shielding Europe's carmakers from Chinese rivals, the EU risks hurting close partners from Turkey and Morocco to Japan and South Korea. Billions in trade and hundreds of thousands of European jobs are at stake.

It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.

Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.

After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.

"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports."

Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.

Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.

The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.

However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all new EU car registrations.

Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.

"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.

Under the revised German-French plan, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.

These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.

They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.

BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.

Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.

For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.

Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.

South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.

Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.

"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he said.

EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.

Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" program, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.

Pardi said this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries]."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.

"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.

Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding."

With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.

"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he said.

#976. Diogo Dalot insists Man United's dramatic comeback against Roma can 'change season'

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Manchester United battled back from two goals down to beat Roma on Tuesday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Diogo Dalot believes Manchester United's dramatic Champions League comeback against Roma can change their season.

United trailed by two goals at Old Trafford on Tuesday before winning a memorable European tie 3-2.

Bruno Fernandes' retaken penalty started the recovery, with a last-gasp Matheus Cunha brace and an even later red card completing a spectacular fightback by Michael Carrick's side.

Roma had raced into a deserved two-goal lead, and a United side in the midst of a nine-match winless run had looked set to see that sequence reach double figures.

That barren spell includes poor Premier League performances, and the Red Devils' worst start to a league campaign since 1986 which has left them 17th, just above the relegation zone on goal difference.

Reflecting on Tuesday’s win, Dalot said: "I think a really good second half. I think we came with the right attitude.

"We did pretty much everything that we needed to do to turn the game on and it's moments like this, it's nights like this that can change momentum, and hopefully we can change ours. Not just the manager, everyone is under pressure.

"When you don't win games for this football club, every moment, every person, everyone involved gets under pressure, and we felt it obviously, because we're not near good enough of what we should have done.

“And, like I said, nights like this can change momentum, can change seasons, and I think this win is going to give us confidence for the next games.”

Attention now turns to Aston Villa's visit to Old Trafford, where United will attempt to follow up the Roma turnaround by winning their second Premier League match of the season.

A victory on Sunday would be huge for all connected to the club ahead of the international break, while further disappointment would darken the mood and raise major questions over Carrick's future.

“These moments are really tough, I’m not going to lie,” Dalot said.

"Unfortunately, I've had a few moments like this in the past, and the only way for us to get out is by winning football games. I think that's the only way you can get confidence.

"And nights like this, like I've said, give you an extra confidence that make you believe that you can create these moments, not just for us, but for the fans.

“And it’s important from everyone around the club feeling that we care, that we want to turn this around, and I think we’ve showed, especially in the second 45 minutes, that we really want to turn this around.”

Dalot's view is that the head start United gave Roma left Carrick's side with “nothing more to lose”, and Villa cannot be handed the same early advantage.

“That’s the unfortunate situation that we are in, so we just had to really go at it,” he said of the second half.

“I think that the biggest thing that we need to get out of this game today is when we play like this, when you have the right attitude, when the fans really believe that we are there, we can be a very strong team.”

#975. Bigger but not better: Why UEFA have killed the early stages of the Champions League

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

League phase games may be entertaining, but that does not matter without jeopardy

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In April 2021, European football faced an existential threat. Twelve of the continent’s biggest clubs announced a plan to break away from the Champions League and form a European Super League, a closed-shop competition designed to guarantee them regular games against each other.

The dirty dozen would not have to qualify and could never be relegated, an affront to the traditions of European football and the principles of sporting fairness. The backlash was swift and fierce, and within days the project was dead in the water.

The Champions League survived, but only after a fundamental overhaul that gave the drivers of the Super League project much of what they wanted. Plans to switch from the old 32-team group stage to a 36-team, Swiss-style league phase had already been cooked up before the Super League news broke, yet the reforms reflected a desire to keep the elite clubs happy. We are now in the third season of this format, enough time to conclude that UEFA’s flagship tournament has been made worse by its introduction.

That is not to say the old group stage was perfect. After 30 years, it had grown stale and predictable. Dead rubbers were common, as dominant teams regularly wrapped up qualification early. Surprise early exits became increasingly rare. The tournament only came to life in the knockout rounds.

Yet the league phase has solved hardly any of those issues while creating new ones of its own. No fewer than 144 matches are required to eliminate just 12 teams, most of whom were expected to bow out early anyway.

The league phase forgives more than a priest in Las Vegas. It is possible to lose five out of eight games, as Benfica did last term, and still reach the knockouts. In 2024/25, PSG won only one of their first five outings yet ended up finishing 15th, before going on to lift the trophy. The margin for error is considerable.

The league phase creates an illusion of direct comparison. In most domestic leagues, you play every team twice. In the Champions League, you are ranked alongside sides who have played entirely different opponents. Some clubs have much tougher fixture lists than others, yet this is not (and cannot be) reflected in the standings.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In theory, there are fewer dead rubbers than before. A top-24 finish is all that is needed to extend your participation beyond the league phase, but there are advantages to ending the campaign as high up the table as possible. The top eight progress directly to the round of 16, while teams finishing between ninth and 16th earn home advantage in the second leg of their knockout phase play-off. Yet the reward for finishing in the top eight - the chance to skip a round - is an odd one. UEFA's biggest incentive to excel in its tournament is to play less of it.

The principal reason the league phase was brought in was to offer more blockbuster clashes early on, which were relatively rare in the old system of eight groups of four. This season we have already seen such titanic tussles as Real Madrid vs Inter, Atletico Madrid vs Manchester United, Manchester City vs PSG, PSG vs Barcelona and Bayern Munich vs Arsenal.

At first glance, these fixtures would appear to have delivered the goods. PSG beat both Manchester City and Barcelona 4-2 in pulsating affairs. Bayern and Arsenal drew 2-2 in a game full of quality at the Allianz Arena. There were chances galore in Real Madrid’s 2-1 victory over Inter on matchday one.

UEFA's biggest incentive to excel in its tournament is to play less of it.

Yet for all the entertainment on show, these encounters were much less gripping than comparable contests in the knockout stage. The football was technically impressive, but the lack of jeopardy left many feeling numb. Significance had been stripped away. Without the feeling that it really means something, a meeting of European heavyweights feels like little more than an exhibition game.

The problem is, both UEFA and the continent’s elite clubs will be happy with the new arrangement. More games means more money for everyone involved. And while there is a risk of losing a couple of matches when you have to play the likes of Real Madrid or Bayern Munich, it is unlikely to put qualification at risk. After all, you can amass enough points to advance by beating Sabah, Viking and Slovan Bratislava.

The Champions League knockout stage remains the pinnacle of the club game. Memorable ties become iconic in a way that is impossible in the league phase. The Champions League will be appointment viewing again once we reach the round of 16. Until then, Europe’s biggest tournament feels strangely inconsequential.

Greg Lea is a freelance football journalist who's filled in wherever FourFourTwo needs him since 2014. He became a Crystal Palace fan after watching a 1-0 loss to Port Vale in 1998, and once got on the scoresheet in a primary school game against Wilfried Zaha's Whitehorse Manor (an own goal in an 8-0 defeat).

Newcastle United's reliance on the past is costing them dearly in the present after another home defeat

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The cruel irony of Newcastle United’s current predicament is that, for all they are looking to the future, they are too reliant on the past and it is costing them dearly in the present.

As the rain lashed down at St James’ Park on Monday night, it captured the sodden mood on Tyneside as Everton secured a third straight Premier League win on that famous ground courtesy of Thierno Barry’s second half goal.

Newcastle dropped to 13th in the table after a third defeat in four.

A sell out crowd greeted the final whistle with the sort of indignation which could be construed in a tipping point in their tolerance of the current state of affairs, something Matthias Jaissle insisted he understood as pressure on him grows.

"I was aware of the anger,” he told reporters afterwards. “Big frustration, big disappointment because we couldn't transfer what we saw in the week.

"The team was training at a high level, but since the ref started the game, not much was seen. It's difficult to understand. Of course the fans are frustrated, like we are.

"Unfortunately, we couldn't deliver. Actually, over the whole 90 minutes, it was not our game and our style of playing. That is something we are very frustrated and disappointed about. If you cannot deliver when it counts, then you don't deserve to win.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

With every passing game, it becomes clearer that the framing of the summer may have been wrong. Newcastle knew there would be huge transition, with the sales of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali accounted for in advance.

The departures first of manager Eddie Howe and then captain Bruno Guimaraes just weeks out from the start of the Premier League season were not what the club wanted.

Yet, in an interview with TNT Sports before the 2-2 draw with Bournemouth on September 5, sporting director Ross Wilson insisted the summer had gone to plan “almost in its entirety”.

Out with the old and in with the new; a refresh, Newcastle 2.0. That is what the fans were told. After the success of the first five years under the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, which yielded two Champions League campaigns and a trophy, Newcastle had hit their ceiling and it was necessary to take a step back to move forward again in a more sustainable manner.

Wilson spoke of giving youth a chance and taking risks - a fresh identity he hoped would help the club become more competitive in the long run. More than £200m was spent on eight new players, but the problem is Jaissle does not seem to count on a number of them.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m, but the 20-year-old Ivorian has barely featured; the same can be said for £35m midfielder Aladji Bamba.

Following a stellar performance in the victory over Hull City on September 19, it was hoped Dutch teenager Sean Steur would be given more responsibility. His substitute appearance shortly after Barry’s opener was his first league appearance since.

The bold strategy set out has yet to come to fruition. It is hard to blame Jaissle for not having more trust, but the upshot is that Guimaraes’ replacement right now looks to be Joe Willock, a player who, it was almost universally felt for as long as a couple of years, had no future at Newcastle.

Replacing Alexander Isak’s goals, a year after his acrimonious departure for Liverpool, is the responsibility of Will Osula, his former understudy, despite £175m being spent on strikers since 2025.

Harvey Barnes, consistently used as a bit-part player while Gordon shone on the left, has been given his opportunity. At present, he simply isn’t taking it.

There are so many others, too. Jaissle brought Fabian Schar and Dan Burn back into the fold ahead of the victory over Crystal Palace last Sunday and it worked perfectly. Since returning from injury, too, Joelinton has been a regular in an unfamiliar deep midfield role, but his physicality and leadership are seen as too important to go without.

Newcastle rejected a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest for Jacob Murphy on transfer deadline day and he too has featured regularly this season.

All of these players were crucial in Newcastle’s recent success, but by complimenting the best players in the team. Now Isak, Guimaraes, Tonali and Gordon have left, making them more prominent naturally reduces the overall quality, and it is not hard to understand the sort of impact that has on progress.

Long-term, the hope is that Steur, Bamba and Toure will develop into players capable of filling the boots of the players who have gone. They certainly have the profile and potential to do so. But right now, there is a void in Newcastle's squad, an imbalance between its character and quality. Left unchecked, the consequences could be dire.

#970. Chelsea star Cole Palmer escaped straight red card against Tottenham, says KMI panel

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents panel also identified missed decisions involving Aston Villa and Fulham, as it reviewed several contentious refereeing calls

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Chelsea forward Cole Palmer ought to have been dismissed ten minutes prior to his eventual sending-off against Tottenham, an independent assessment panel reviewing Premier League refereeing and VAR decisions has concluded.

Following an altercation between Palmer and Spurs player Mateus Fernandes during the 70th minute at Stamford Bridge on October 24, the Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel determined that the England international deserved a straight red card.

By a 3-2 majority, the five-member panel decided that referee Chris Kavanagh's initial call on the pitch was mistaken. Three panellists viewed Palmer's challenge on Fernandes as violent conduct warranting dismissal, noting there was "clear contact to the head" along with behaviour deemed "unnecessary, dangerous and made with excessive force".

Nevertheless, all five panellists agreed with VAR John Brooks's choice to refrain from advising an on-field review, backing his decision to stand by the original yellow card awarded by the match official.

Palmer was ultimately ordered off ten minutes later in the 80th minute after receiving a second booking following a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In a separate evaluation from the same day, the KMI panel judged that Aston Villa ought to have been awarded a spot-kick during their victory against Manchester City after Elliot Anderson tangled with Johan Manzambi.

Three members of the panel argued that Anderson made no effort to play the ball and intentionally widened his posture to block Manzambi's path.

Although a 3-2 majority felt the VAR was correct not to intervene with a review recommendation, two panel members contended that a clear and obvious error had occurred.

According to Premier League figures, 88 per cent of 162 key incidents evaluated by the panel this season were correctly judged on the pitch, matching performance levels from the same phase last year. That accuracy rate rises to 99 per cent once VAR intervention is taken into account.

Examining the fixture between Coventry and Fulham, the panel noted that VAR Jarred Gillett should have prompted referee Adam Herczeg to check a late first-half incident, despite agreeing with the ultimate outcome reached on the pitch and in the video room that no penalty be given to Fulham.

It noted an impactful hold by Fulham's Calvin Bassey prior to the corner kick being taken, succeeded by an infringement from Coventry's Bradley Thomas-Asante once the ball entered play. The panel accepted that the VAR had properly spotted both offences.

In its findings, the panel explained: "In this situation, as Bassey commits an offence before the ball is in play and the holding action of Thomas-Asante met the threshold for a penalty to be awarded, the VAR should recommend an on-field review to allow the referee to consider both holding actions and reach the correct outcome of retaken corner."

The Premier League is currently participating in an International Football Association Board trial that permits video officials to step in if an attacking player commits a pre-kick-off foul at set-pieces that directly affects a goal, penalty, or red-card decision.

The iconic former Reds forward and manager had a strange day out at Anfield back in 1995 with his Blackburn side going for the title

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You couldn't have written it. On the final day of the 1994/95 Premier League season, Kenny Dalglish returned in front of the Anfield crowd that adored him and were cheering him on - but as manager of their opposition, Blackburn Rovers, who needed results to go their way to win the league.

The situation was this: if Blackburn lost, and Manchester United won away to West Ham, then Alex Ferguson's side would win the title at Rovers' expense. Indeed, Ferguson openly suggested that Liverpool may be less than up for the occasion.

But the now-Sir Kenny believes the now-Sir Alex was absolutely entitled to push that agenda - and that, in fact, he wouldn't have been doing his job properly if he hadn't.

As it happened, Blackburn did lose... but Man United could only draw at West Ham, thus handing the title to Blackburn. Sir Kenny recently told FourFourTwo: “In 1994-95, we were competing against Manchester United for the title, but there was no animosity between me and Alex Ferguson.

"As managers, you were in competition with everybody; what's wrong with that? He was going to speak up for his club, to put ideas into people's minds or dismiss other people's ideas, and I was the same.

"If you weren't supporting your club, the punters were going to be unhappy, so he had every right to do it. He was as good as gold.

"The last game of the season was at Anfield – it was always amazing to go back to Anfield, and the Liverpool punters wanted us to win that day.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"It's not often that they go to Anfield and want the opposition to win, is it?

"If you're not going to win the league at home, then for me, that was a fairy tale to win it at Anfield.

"The TV people wouldn't tell us what the score was from Manchester United's game at West Ham, but people were cheering when their game finished, and it came to pass that we were champions.

"You think about where a lot of those boys were before, and we didn't have a great deal of experience of players winning trophies for previous teams.

"But it was just, ‘Get on with it, you are where you are because you deserve to be there, so just do your best.'

"When I saw Jack Walker after the game, he couldn't speak.

"He'd played a huge, huge part in the financial support, and he never, ever interfered.

"To see somebody of his business strength in tears, you'd think he'd done something wrong - but they were tears of joy

#967. Fruit, flies and getting frisky: how food odours trigger sexual arousal

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Thomas O. Auer is in the Department of Biology and at the Food Research and Innovation Center, University of Fribourg, 1700 Fribourg, Switzerland.

When the goddess Hera set out to seduce Zeus in Homer’s The Iliad, she did not start with her looks, but with perfume, preparing an ambrosial oil with a fragrance that filled “heaven and Earth”. The idea that scent kindles desire still captures our imaginations, but how odours act on the human brain to drive sexual attraction is unclear, and decades of searching for sex pheromones have produced no convincing candidates. That is not the case for insects, in which chemical sex signals are well understood. Writing in Nature, Brand et al.1 add another piece to the mosaic of sexual communication. By comparing fly species that are adapted to different host fruits, they show that food odours can be key for male sexual arousal. Flies combine this cue with information about their social environment to get into the mood for mating.

Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has agreed his next transfer.

The Argentine centre-back was sent off at the weekend for Man United against Chelsea in manager Michael Carrick's third successive defeat, in what is fast becoming a nightmare campaign at the club.

It follows comments that Martinez made criticising the Red Devils' hierarchy, as things begin to unravel at Old Trafford.

Martinez joined Manchester United from Ajax in 2022 in a move worth £57 million, as reported by the BBC, with the Red Devils beating Arsenal to the signing of the defender and then-manager Erik ten Hag reuniting with one of his generals from the Johan Cruyff Arena.

Martinez has shown good form at times during his four years in Manchester, though concerns over the 5ft 9in centre-back's height have persisted during his time in English football.

Recent errors and controversy, meanwhile, have led to rumours that the World Cup winner could be for the chop, after being hauled off at half-time against Leeds United, being excluded from Carrick's squad against Como, and only featuring as a substitute in the defeat to Bournemouth.

Now, Fichajes in Spain has cited insiders in a report saying Martinez has reached a “preliminary agreement” on personal terms to join Atletico Madrid.

While FourFourTwo understands that Martinez is still some way off from a full agreement for his exit from United, both player and employer appear to be content to go their separate ways as soon as possible.

Jesus Owono was sent off after colliding with De Miguel, who died in hospital on Tuesday after suffering a cardiac arrest
